### A collision in 2009 as the origin of the debris trail of asteroid P/2010 A2

**C. Snodgrass, C. Tubiana, J.-B. Vincent and collaborators**

*Nature*, 467, 814–816 (2010).

The paper concluded that the trail resulted from a single event around
10 February 2009 rather than sustained cometary activity.

- [Nature article](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09453)
- [ESA Rosetta image and mission context](https://sci.esa.int/web/rosetta/-/47829-rosetta-image-of-the-asteroid-p-2010-a2)

Overview

P/2010 A2 was discovered by the LINEAR survey in January 2010 as an unusual object in the inner main asteroid belt. It appeared to have a long, diffuse trail resembling a cometary tail, yet it showed no clear coma or central condensation associated with ordinary cometary activity.

The object quickly became a target of interest because its orbit was asteroidal, while its visible appearance suggested dust loss. Early interpretations considered whether it could be a main-belt comet: an asteroid whose visible activity is driven by sublimating volatile material.

Subsequent observations revealed a small surviving nucleus separated from the main dust trail. This made a different explanation plausible: the visible structure could be debris created by a recent collision between asteroids.

This collaborative project used a rare observation from ESA’s Rosetta spacecraft, together with ground-based telescope imaging and dust-dynamics modelling, to determine the origin of the trail.

Research question

Was P/2010 A2 an active main-belt comet, or was its trail produced by a single impact event?

A related aim was to establish when the dust was released and to constrain the properties of the particles shaping the visible trail.

Why Rosetta mattered

From Earth, P/2010 A2 was observed from a relatively limited range of viewing angles. Several physical scenarios could produce similar projected trail shapes, making it difficult to determine whether the observed dust arose from ongoing cometary activity or an impulsive collision.

Rosetta provided a unique vantage point.

In March 2010, the spacecraft was travelling through the asteroid belt on its route to comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Its orbit was inclined relative to P/2010 A2’s, allowing the OSIRIS camera system to view the object from a substantially different phase angle than was available from Earth.

Although P/2010 A2 was faint in the Rosetta images, this alternative geometry was decisive. Combined with observations from Earth, it enabled the research team to constrain the three-dimensional form and evolution of the debris trail.

Observations

Rosetta/OSIRIS

The object was observed on 16 March 2010 using the OSIRIS Narrow Angle Camera on ESA’s Rosetta spacecraft.

The OSIRIS images showed the dust trail from a perspective unavailable to ground-based observatories. This made it possible to test whether the trail geometry was consistent with continuous emission from an active comet or with material released in a single impact.

Ground-based observations

Rosetta data were compared with complementary ground-based imaging, including observations from the New Technology Telescope and Palomar Observatory.

The combined dataset extended the available viewing geometry and supported a more robust reconstruction of the dust distribution.

Method

The team used Finson-Probstein dust-dynamics modelling to simulate the appearance of dust released from P/2010 A2.

The method models how dust particles move under the combined effects of solar gravity and solar-radiation pressure. A key parameter is beta, the ratio of solar-radiation-pressure acceleration to solar gravitational acceleration.

By varying:

  • The date of dust emission.
  • The initial particle distribution.
  • Particle-size-related beta values.
  • The viewing geometry.
  • The expected effects of radiation pressure over time.

the team generated model trails for comparison with Rosetta and ground-based images.

The distinctive Rosetta viewing angle reduced the number of viable solutions. A single, impulsive release of dust provided the best match to the observations.

Findings

The combined observations and modelling showed that P/2010 A2’s trail was not produced by prolonged cometary activity.

Instead, the trail was consistent with debris released in a single asteroid collision. The preferred solution placed the event around 10 February 2009, with an uncertainty window of approximately 10 days.

The analysis indicated that the visible trail contained relatively large dust particles, broadly millimetre to centimetre scale, that remained close to the parent body. The geometry could be explained by an impact that ejected clumps of debris, which subsequently dispersed under the influence of solar gravity and radiation pressure.

This work provided direct evidence for a recent collision in the asteroid belt and offered an unusual opportunity to study the early evolution of an asteroid impact debris field.

My role

I contributed as part of the University of Kent group within the wider Rosetta/OSIRIS collaboration.

The research drew on expertise from institutions across Europe and the United States, combining spacecraft imaging, ground-based observation, dust-dynamics modelling and interpretation of small-body activity.

The collaboration included researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research, University of Kent, ESA, Queen’s University Belfast, Jet Propulsion Laboratory and other partner institutions.

Significance

Asteroid collisions are fundamental to the evolution of the Solar System, but they are difficult to observe shortly after they occur.

P/2010 A2 was significant because its debris remained visible soon after a recent event. The system therefore provided an opportunity to examine how impact ejecta evolves into a dust trail under solar radiation pressure and orbital motion.

The work also demonstrated the value of multi-vantage-point astronomy. Rosetta was not originally designed to study P/2010 A2, but its position in the Solar System supplied the crucial perspective needed to distinguish between competing interpretations.

Limitations

The dust trail was observed after the collision rather than at the moment of impact. Reconstructing the event therefore depended on models of dust motion, assumptions about particle properties and comparisons between images obtained at different times and viewing angles.

The modelling strongly supported an impulsive collision, but it did not provide a direct image of the impacting object or a complete measurement of the collision’s initial conditions. Estimates of particle sizes and release geometry remain model-dependent.

## Overview

**Pan-STARRS (Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System)** is an array of astronomical telescopes, cameras, and computing equipment that surveys the sky on a continual basis.

[PSWWW](http://pswww.ifa.hawaii.edu/pswww/)
The Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System, located at Haleakalā Observatory, Hawaii, US, consists of astronomical cameras, telescopes, and a computing facility that surveys the sky for moving or variable objects on a continual basis. It also produces accurate astrometry and photometry of already-detected objects.

## Campaign results

In the end, we found **13 possible candidates**, which didn't quite beat our record of **22** earlier in the year. Hopefully we can smash that target next time!

To date, we have **5 preliminary discoveries** from this campaign, with hopefully more to follow.

## International Astronomical Search Collaboration

The **[International Astronomical Search Collaboration (IASC)](https://iasc.cosmosearch.org/)** is a citizen science programme that provides high-quality astronomical data to citizen scientists around the world.

These citizen scientists are able to make original astronomical discoveries and participate in hands-on astronomy. The service is provided at no cost.

### Asteroid search campaigns

Asteroid Search Campaigns are the primary focus of IASC. A **campaign** is a month-long event in which teams search for asteroids using astronomical observations and analysis tools.

If you are new to IASC and would like more information about participating in asteroid search campaigns, visit the [**IASC registration page**](https://iasc.cosmosearch.org/Home/Registration).

## Discoveries

This campaign produced five preliminary discoveries to date, demonstrating the value of citizen science in identifying previously unconfirmed moving objects within astronomical survey data.

The search also contributed to the wider effort to identify and track near-Earth objects and other small Solar System bodies through systematic analysis of survey observations.

I took part as a member of a UKSEDS asteroid-search team during the campaign.

A University of Leicester student CubeSat mission designed to investigate the near-Earth dust environment using an active nanometeoroid detector.
Supported communications for a University of Leicester student CubeSat designed to measure near-Earth nanometeoroid dust.

## Overview

**PLUME — the Detector Picosatellite of Leicester University Micrometeoroid Experiment —** was a student-led CubeSat project at the University of Leicester designed to investigate the near-Earth space-dust environment.

The project began in **January 2007** and brought together undergraduate students, academic researchers and industry partners to design, build and prepare a small satellite for launch.

The mission aimed to demonstrate that students could take responsibility for a complete space mission, from initial concept and spacecraft design through to communications, payload development and launch.

## Mission overview

PLUME was developed by undergraduate students in the University of Leicester's **Department of Physics and Astronomy**, with support from the University's **Space Research Centre** and engineering company **Magna Parva Ltd**.

The mission was intended to place an active nanometeoroid detector into orbit by **mid-2009**.

At the time, the project was expected to potentially become the **first English CubeSat in orbit**.

The spacecraft was being developed to the **CubeSat standard**, originally developed by California Polytechnic State University and Stanford University.

More than simply an educational exercise, PLUME was intended to produce useful scientific measurements of the near-Earth dust environment.

## Student-led space engineering

Around **20 University of Leicester undergraduate students** were involved in the mission.

The project gave students the opportunity to work across the complete spacecraft lifecycle, including:

- Mission conception
- Spacecraft systems engineering
- Payload development
- Mechanical design
- Electronics
- Attitude determination and control
- Communications
- Telemetry
- Software
- Testing
- Launch preparation

The project was notable for giving undergraduate students direct responsibility for developing hardware intended for a real space mission.

As Philip Peterson, a second-year undergraduate working on the Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS), described it:

> "I'm an undergraduate, and I'm building a satellite. It's just incredible."

The project therefore served both a scientific purpose and an important educational role, providing students with practical experience of spacecraft development and the professional environment of the space industry.

## Industry collaboration

PLUME was supported by **Magna Parva Ltd**, an engineering company based in Loughborough.

Magna Parva donated the main body of the spacecraft and worked with the student team throughout the project.

Andrew Bowyer, Director of Magna Parva, described the company's involvement as extending beyond financial support, with the intention of working with the students through to launch.

This industry–university model was intended to give students practical experience alongside their academic education.

The project also had the support of the **University of Leicester Space Research Centre**, with the **East Midlands Space Academy** considered as a potential source of financial support.

## The science case

Space dust is found throughout the Solar System and is an important component of the near-Earth environment.

Dust contributes to phenomena including the **zodiacal light**, with thermal emission from space dust particularly prominent at infrared wavelengths.

The PLUME science case distinguished between naturally occurring **space dust** and human-generated **orbital debris**.

### Space dust

Space dust is naturally occurring material originating from sources such as:

- Comets
- Asteroids
- Collisions between Solar System bodies
- Interplanetary dust populations

### Orbital debris

Orbital debris, by contrast, is predominantly human-made material associated with spacecraft and launch systems.

Although their origins differ, both dust and debris can interact with spacecraft at extremely high velocities.

Impact velocities can exceed:

**20 km/s**

At these velocities, even extremely small particles can produce significant effects.

## Why measure near-Earth dust?

Understanding the near-Earth dust population has implications for both fundamental science and spacecraft engineering.

Better measurements can contribute to:

- Understanding the distribution of interplanetary dust
- Modelling the near-Earth environment
- Spacecraft risk assessment
- Understanding micrometeoroid impacts
- Designing future spacecraft and instruments
- Investigating dusty plasma environments

The PLUME team aimed to improve the characterisation of very small particles beyond the capabilities of previous active detectors.

The proposed detector was intended to provide measurements of particles down to approximately **20 nm** in diameter.

## Dusty plasmas

Charged dust grains can interact strongly with surrounding plasma.

Dusty plasma environments are relevant to a number of astrophysical and planetary systems, including the terrestrial magnetosphere and planetary ring systems.

The PLUME science case highlighted research into the role of dusty plasmas in:

- Magnetosphere dynamics
- Plasma interactions
- Planetary rings
- Space environments containing charged particulate matter

The interaction between dust and plasma therefore provides an additional scientific motivation for understanding the population of small particles in space.

## Spacecraft risk

Micrometeoroids are also an important consideration for spacecraft and scientific instruments.

The PLUME science case highlighted damage observed on the **XMM-Newton** and **Swift** missions, where micrometeoroid impacts affected CCD detectors.

Open-optics instruments can be particularly vulnerable to dust impacts because particles can reach sensitive optical and detector surfaces.

A better understanding of the near-Earth dust population can therefore contribute to spacecraft and instrument risk assessment.

## The PLUME detector

The central scientific instrument was an active nanometeoroid detector based on **microchannel plates (MCPs)**.

The detector used **two microchannel plates covered with an aluminium nanofilm**.

Similar detector technology had previously been flown on the **International Space Station**, where returned MCPs were examined for impact features.

The thin aluminium film was highly sensitive to very small particle impacts.

The proposed PLUME detector had a minimum detectable particle diameter of approximately:

**~20 nm**

## Microchannel plate detection

The detector used the physical effects produced when a hypervelocity dust particle strikes the thin aluminium-coated MCP surface.

An impact capable of producing a detectable hole or impact feature can generate a plasma.

When a high voltage is applied across the MCP, this plasma can initiate an electron cascade.

The resulting electron multiplication provides a measurable electrical signal corresponding to the particle impact.

The basic detection chain was:

**Particle impact → plasma generation → electron cascade → electrical pulse → signal processing → spacecraft computer**

## Signal processing

The detector electronics were designed to convert the very small impact event into a measurable voltage signal.

A typical impact was expected to produce approximately:

**~50,000 electrons**

The pre-amplifier converted this signal into an approximately:

**~16 mV exponentially decaying voltage pulse**

The signal was then processed by a shaping amplifier.

A peak-sample-and-hold circuit stored the signal amplitude and generated an interrupt for the spacecraft computer.

The computer then:

1. Collected the event data.
2. Recorded the signal information.
3. Cleared the buffer.
4. Prepared the detector electronics for the next event.

A **commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) ultra-light high-voltage power supply** was used to generate the voltage required by the MCP detector.

## Detector specifications

The proposed detector had the following characteristics:

| Parameter | Specification |
| --- | ---: |
| Detector body diameter | 33 mm |
| Active detector diameter | 25 mm |
| MCP diameter | 33 mm |
| MCP aluminium film | 40 nm |
| MCP pore size | 12.5 µm |
| Detector body mass | ~15 g |
| Detector mass budget | 211 g |
| Detector volume | 90 cm³ |
| Average power | 966 mW |
| Detectability limit | ~20 nm |

The extremely small detection threshold was one of the key scientific advantages proposed for PLUME.

## MCP technology

The detector's MCPs were coated with an aluminium film.

The technology drew on earlier work demonstrating that very thin films can reveal the effects of extremely small particle impacts.

Previous MCP experiments had shown impact features in aluminium films only tens of nanometres thick.

For PLUME, the detector concept used:

- **33 mm diameter MCPs**
- **40 nm aluminium coating**
- **12.5 µm pore size**
- High-voltage electron multiplication
- Electronic pulse detection

This provided a lightweight detector architecture suitable for a CubeSat-scale spacecraft.

## Communications and telemetry

The mission also provided an opportunity for students to work on spacecraft communications and telemetry.

Professor George Fraser invited **Andy Thomas** to act as a mentor for the PLUME up-link and down-link systems.

Thomas brought previous experience in satellite telemetry analysis, including work involving:

- LUSAT
- STARSHINE 3
- QUAKESAT

His archive documents experiments with decoding satellite telemetry and analysing spacecraft housekeeping data.

The PLUME communications work therefore built on established amateur and research satellite telemetry techniques.

The project also involved **John Heath (G7HIA)** as a fellow communications mentor.

## Student engineering experience

One of the defining characteristics of PLUME was its emphasis on genuine student ownership.

Rather than treating the spacecraft as a purely theoretical academic exercise, students were involved in developing hardware and systems intended for a real space mission.

This provided experience across disciplines including:

- Physics
- Astronomy
- Electronics
- Computing
- Mechanical engineering
- Spacecraft systems
- Communications
- Instrumentation
- Project management

The project demonstrated how CubeSats could provide universities with a relatively accessible route into practical spacecraft development.

## A cubesat for Leicester

The PLUME project emerged during an important period in the development of university CubeSat missions.

Small satellites offered universities the opportunity to develop and test space hardware without the scale and cost associated with conventional spacecraft programmes.

For Leicester students, PLUME represented an opportunity to move from studying space science to actually building a spacecraft.

The mission combined:

**Student education + scientific research + spacecraft engineering + industry collaboration**

## Project timeline

### January 2007

The University of Leicester CubeSat project began.

### 2007–2008

Students developed the spacecraft and payload, supported by academics and industry partners.

### June 2008

The University of Leicester announced that the student team had taken delivery of the spacecraft's main body, donated by Magna Parva.

At this stage, the mission was targeting an orbital launch in 2009.

### January 2009

The PLUME detector and science case were presented at the **2nd European CubeSat Workshop at ESTEC**.

The presentation described the scientific motivation, MCP detector technology, electronics and spacecraft budgets.

### Mid-2009

The original mission plan targeted deployment of the CubeSat into orbit.

## Legacy

PLUME represents an early example of the growing role of **student-built CubeSats in UK space education and research**.

The project combined a scientifically interesting payload with a practical educational model in which students participated in the development of an actual spacecraft.

Its emphasis on very small particle detection also illustrates how CubeSats can provide platforms for focused scientific experiments that would otherwise require much larger missions.

The project brought together:

- University research
- Undergraduate education
- Space instrumentation
- Industry expertise
- Amateur satellite communications
- CubeSat engineering

## My role

I supported PLUME as its volunteer communications officer, helping to explain the mission and its science to wider audiences.

Opened up practical training in Galileo-enabled IoT business and technical development to anyone, supporting a wider pipeline of European IoT entrepreneurs beyond the teams selected for the POINT.IoT acceleration programme.

## Overview

Point.MOOC is the online training element of **POINT.IoT**, an EU-funded
programme designed to stimulate innovation at the intersection of the Internet
of Things (IoT) and European satellite navigation (EGNSS, including Galileo).

The course exists because the programme believes everyone should have access
to the tools needed to support Galileo-enabled IoT solutions. It is a
self-directed, free training programme that lets entrepreneurs develop their
ideas at their own pace, whether they are new to the field or already
established in IoT or Galileo-related business.

## Background: the POINT.IoT programme

POINT.IoT was funded under Horizon 2020 and organised by leading companies
including Verhaert, SpaceTec Partners, Cesah and Orange, with support from the
European GNSS Agency (now EUSPA). It combined several strands:

- **POINT.Cheetah:** scouting and selecting new IoT applications that use GNSS
  technologies for a three-month technical and business sprint with a
  multidisciplinary team of mentors.
- **POINT.Kangeroo:** business training tools to support the teams, including
  the POINT.IoT Entrepreneur Playbook and the MOOC.
- **POINT.MOOC:** a Massive Open Online Course teaching the business basics in
  a modern, interactive way.
- **POINT.Partnerships:** connecting teams with industrial stakeholders as
  development partners, suppliers, clients or investors.

The MOOC broadened the reach of the programme, giving anyone with an idea
access to the same core knowledge shared with selected teams.

## The challenge

Entrepreneurs building Galileo-enabled IoT products face two linked problems:

- Many have a strong idea or technology but limited experience designing a
  viable business around it.
- Others understand business but are unsure where to start with satellite
  positioning, low-power GNSS or Galileo integration.

Point.MOOC was designed to address both in one structured programme, so that
participants could move from an initial idea to a more robust product concept
and business case.

## Course structure

Point.MOOC takes learners through two connected parts, presented as 14
on-demand training sessions in the course introduction (the full curriculum
lists 18 lessons including two welcome modules).

### Part 1: Business design

Learners journey through the customer problem, product concept design,
business model creation and launching a product:

1. Welcome to the business design sessions
2. Understanding your customer and the product-market fit
3. Developing your IoT value proposition
4. Translating customer requirements into technical concept design
5. Creating your Minimum Viable Product (MVP)
6. Designing and differentiating your user-centred product
7. Creating your business model
8. Taking your product to market
9. How to fund your development

### Part 2: Technical training

The technical sessions explain positioning in our connected world and go deep
into Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) and the European system,
Galileo:

10. Welcome to the technical sessions
11. How does positioning work for the Internet of Things?
12. Using low-power GNSS technologies for your IoT solution
13. The advantages of GNSS positioning
14. What differentiates Galileo?
15. The benefits of processing your GNSS data in the cloud
16. Key technologies for IoT trackers
17. Edge computing
18. Security in IoT and edge computing

## Who it is for

- New entrepreneurs exploring an IoT or location-based idea.
- Established IoT or Galileo businesses looking to strengthen their business
  model or technical approach.
- Developers who want a practical introduction to GNSS and Galileo for IoT
  devices.
- Teams preparing to apply to programmes such as POINT.IoT.

## Instructors

The course brought together business and technical experts from across the
European ecosystem.

**Business experts**

- Annekatrien Debien, Manager, SpaceTec Partners
- Piotr Bucki, Lead Start-Up Mentor, SpaceTec Partners
- Zane Smilga, Coordinator, Open Lab, Verhaert
- Rogelio Chovet, Business Consultant, Verhaert
- David Pas, Coordinator, Designlab, Verhaert

**Technical experts**

- Felix Rottmann, Senior Consultant, SpaceTec Partners
- Miquel Garcia-Fernandez, Co-Founder and CTO, Rokubun
- Xavier Banque Casanovas, Co-Founder, Rokubun

## My role

I contributed to the course through Design & Data, working with SpaceTec Partners on the POINT.IoT programme.

## Significance

Satellite navigation is becoming a foundational layer of the connected world,
but turning it into successful products requires both technical understanding
and sound business design. By making that training free and on-demand, Point.MOOC
lowered the barrier to entry for European IoT start-ups and helped spread
knowledge of Galileo's advantages for positioning, velocity and timing,
particularly in demanding urban environments.

## Overview

**Riga airTEXT** is a free public service that provides air-quality forecasts
for Riga, Latvia. It was designed to help residents and visitors understand
local conditions and prepare for short periods of poor air quality.

The service brings together Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (**CAMS**)
information, satellite observations and high-resolution urban modelling. It
delivers forecasts up to three days ahead through its website, mobile
application, social channels and free SMS or email alerts.

I contributed editorial and science-communication work through Design & Data,
supporting a clear public story about how atmospheric data can become useful,
timely information for a city and its residents.

## The challenge

Air pollution is both technical and personal.

The underlying science involves atmospheric chemistry, emissions, satellite
observations, weather patterns, numerical forecasting and local dispersion
models. But the people who need the information may simply want to know whether
conditions will affect a journey, outdoor activity, child, respiratory illness
or allergy symptoms.

The communication challenge was therefore to translate a complex technical
system into a practical public-service question:

> What will air quality be like where I am, and what should I know before I go
> outside?

The project needed to make the scientific infrastructure credible without
overwhelming the audience with scientific jargon.

## Riga airTEXT

Riga airTEXT launched at Riga City Hall on 27 February 2018. It provides
regularly updated, three-day forecasts for air quality, ultraviolet radiation,
pollen concentrations and air temperature.

The service was developed by UK and Latvian scientists from Cambridge
Environmental Research Consultants (**CERC**) and Estonian, Latvian &
Lithuanian Environment (**ELLE**), with financial support from CAMS. Riga City
Council and Latvia’s environmental authorities worked with the project team to
ensure the service addressed local public needs.

## Forecast information

Riga airTEXT presents local forecast information through multiple channels:

- A public website.
- A mobile application.
- Free SMS alerts.
- Email alerts.
- Facebook and Twitter updates.
- Local air-quality maps and bulletins.

The service uses an air-quality index based on the pollutant expected to have
the greatest health impact on a given day and location. Its public index covers
nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), particulate matter
(PM10 and PM2.5) and ozone
(O₃).

## Technical foundation

The forecasting system combines several complementary sources of information:

- Satellite observations
- CAMS regional air-quality forecasts
- Meteorological forecasts
- High-resolution urban dispersion modelling

Together, these sources produce local public air-quality forecasts.

## My role

I worked as an **Editor and science communicator** through Design & Data.

My contribution included:

- Developing editorial communication for an ECMWF and CAMS user story.
- Explaining local air-quality forecasting for non-specialist audiences.
- Connecting Copernicus atmospheric information with urban public-health needs.
- Supporting multimedia communication associated with the service.

## Outcomes

The work presented Riga airTEXT as a practical example of public-facing environmental data, supported by a short video and presented as part of the European State of the Climate 2017 showcase.

## Limitations

This project concerned editorial communication. It did not involve developing the airTEXT service, running its dispersion models or producing CAMS forecasts.

Air-quality forecasts are subject to uncertainty, particularly at street level, and public communication should explain both their usefulness and their limits.

- [Watch on YouTube](https://youtu.be/1r3QI88w4BI?is=6elRbvBmc2HJFfKH)
- [Riga airTEXT case study on the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/airtext-air-quality-information-glance)

## Related work

This project is part of wider ECMWF and Copernicus communications work on climate services, environmental data and the practical use of Earth observation.

## Overview

**Rosetta Shop** was an online shop associated with the European Space Agency’s
Rosetta mission and its Philae comet lander.

The initiative gave members of the public a way to engage with one of Europe’s
most widely followed space-science missions through mission-related products and
merchandise. My role focused on the practical digital operations that made the
shop work: maintaining the website, keeping product information current and
managing customer orders.

Rosetta was ESA’s comet-chasing mission to comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. It
delivered the Philae lander to the comet’s surface as part of the first detailed
in-situ investigation of a cometary nucleus.

## The context

Rosetta and Philae captured public attention by bringing a complex,
long-duration space mission into everyday conversation.

The mission combined striking scientific imagery, ambitious exploration goals
and a recognisable visual identity. That public interest created an opportunity
to extend mission communication beyond news, social media and educational
materials into tangible products that supporters could buy and share.

The Rosetta Shop served as part of that wider public-engagement ecosystem,
connecting the mission’s visual culture and storytelling with an accessible
e-commerce experience.

## My role

I worked as **Website and Order Manager** through Design & Data.

My responsibilities included:

- Managing the day-to-day operation of the Rosetta Shop website.
- Maintaining product pages, descriptions and catalogue information.
- Processing and coordinating customer orders.
- Monitoring order status and supporting fulfilment workflows.
- Helping ensure that shop information remained accurate and current.
- Supporting customer experience across the purchase and delivery process.
- Coordinating the operational work required for a public-facing online shop.

This role combined editorial care, digital administration and operational
attention to detail.

## Website management

A public-facing shop needs more than an attractive front end. Product listings
must be clear, stock and availability information must be accurate, purchase
paths must work reliably and customers must receive understandable updates.

My website-management work focused on maintaining a clear and dependable
experience for visitors, including:

- Publishing and updating product content.
- Reviewing product descriptions and imagery.
- Maintaining navigation and shop structure.
- Checking that information was current and understandable.
- Supporting the connection between website listings and order workflows.
- Identifying and resolving routine operational issues.

## Order management

Order management was a central part of the work.

The process extended beyond receiving an order. It required coordinating the
information and actions needed to move from purchase to fulfilment while
maintaining a clear record of customer requests and order status.

Key activities included:

- Reviewing incoming customer orders.
- Checking order details and product availability.
- Coordinating fulfilment and dispatch processes.
- Monitoring order progress.
- Responding to customer queries where required.
- Maintaining accurate information across the website and order records.

This operational work helped ensure that the shop matched the standards expected
of an ESA-related public engagement initiative.

## Communications value

The Rosetta Shop was not simply a retail channel. It supported public
engagement with an important European space-science mission.

Mission merchandise can help audiences form a lasting connection with a project
that may otherwise feel distant, technical or inaccessible. Products, visual
identity and storytelling can carry a mission beyond the moment of a launch,
landing or scientific announcement.

For Rosetta, this mattered because the mission had already become a powerful
example of how space exploration, design and public communication can reinforce
one another.

## Outcomes

The project delivered a managed online shop for Rosetta-related merchandise and
public engagement.

Key outcomes included:

- A maintained public-facing website.
- Updated product and catalogue information.
- Coordinated handling of customer orders.
- Support for a reliable purchase-to-fulfilment process.
- An additional route for audiences to connect with Rosetta and Philae.

## Legacy

Rosetta remains one of ESA’s landmark science missions. Its exploration of
comet 67P and deployment of Philae made it a defining public moment for
European space science. ESA continues to present Rosetta and Philae as central
parts of its space-science history.

ESA also maintains official merchandise retailing through its broader ESA Shop,
which presents ESA-branded products celebrating European space ambitions.

## Limitations

My contribution was operational rather than scientific or spacecraft-related.

I did not design the Rosetta spacecraft, develop mission instruments or lead
ESA’s science communications. Instead, I helped sustain an online platform that
made the mission’s public-facing identity accessible through a functioning,
well-managed e-commerce service.

The role required balancing two forms of responsibility:

- **Digital quality:** accurate, usable and well-maintained website content.
- **Operational reliability:** careful handling of orders and customer
  expectations.

## Related work

This project is part of wider Design & Data work supporting ESA mission
communications, digital experiences and public engagement.

## Overview

**Rosetta Strato** was a digital campaign built around the story of ESA's
**Rosetta mission** and the **Philae lander**.

bring the mission to a wider audience. It connected the scientific and

## The mission story

ESA's Rosetta mission became one of the defining planetary-science missions of
its era, travelling to and studying a comet and deploying the Philae lander to
its surface.

The mission provided an unusually compelling story for public engagement:
a spacecraft travelling across the Solar System, rendezvousing with a comet and
attempting a controlled landing on a small, active planetary body.

Rosetta and Philae therefore provided both a scientific subject and a powerful
communications narrative.

The Rosetta Strato campaign built on this story to create a more accessible
public-facing experience.

## Campaign purpose

The campaign was intended to translate a complex space mission into an
engaging digital story.

Rather than presenting the mission only through technical information, the
project focused on the human-readable narrative surrounding Rosetta and
Philae.

The campaign combined:

- Space-science storytelling
- Digital design
- Visual communication
- Educational engagement
- Public outreach
- Campaign promotion
- Charity fundraising

This made the project both a communications exercise and an example of using
space exploration as a vehicle for public engagement.

## Communication approach

The campaign centred on the idea that the story of a space mission can be made
accessible without removing the scientific context.

Rosetta and Philae offered a particularly strong narrative structure because
the mission contained clear stages and moments of public interest: the journey
through space, arrival at the comet, deployment of Philae and the subsequent
scientific and engineering challenges.

The digital campaign therefore used the mission itself as the organising
narrative.

The emphasis was on making the subject visually engaging and understandable
for audiences who might not otherwise encounter detailed planetary-science
material.

## Design

Design was central to the project.

The visual treatment was intended to create an immediate connection with the
Rosetta and Philae story while providing a clear route through the campaign
content.

The project demonstrates how visual design can support science communication
by providing a framework through which complex subjects can be explored.

The campaign imagery and associated digital material provided a recognisable
identity for the project while retaining the connection to the underlying
mission.

## Digital campaign

The project was developed as a digital campaign rather than simply as a static
information page.

The campaign connected visual material, mission storytelling and external
resources to provide audiences with multiple ways of engaging with the
Rosetta/Philae story.

The campaign included a video component and was associated with a charitable
campaign hosted through Indiegogo.

The Rosetta and Philae story naturally lends itself to education because it
connects fundamental scientific concepts with a real space mission.

The campaign provided an opportunity to communicate subjects including:

- Cometary science
- Spacecraft exploration
- Planetary science
- Space engineering
- Mission operations
- Scientific discovery
- The challenges of operating spacecraft far from Earth

The project therefore demonstrates how a contemporary space mission can be
used as the basis for informal science education and public engagement.

international educational initiative focused on using astronomy and space to
inspire and educate young people.

## Role of storytelling

One of the central lessons from the project is the value of narrative in
science communication.

A space mission contains an enormous amount of technical information, but
audiences do not necessarily engage with technical information simply because
it is available.

Rosetta and Philae already possessed a compelling narrative. The role of the
campaign was to make that narrative accessible through design and digital
communication.

This approach helps bridge the gap between:

**scientific achievement → understandable story → public engagement**

## My role

I contributed through Design & Data, combining design, digital communication and space-science storytelling.

The project brought together:

- Digital campaign development
- Visual communication
- Science education and public engagement
- Charity campaigning
- Video communication

## Outcomes

The project resulted in a public-facing campaign centred on Rosetta and
Philae, supported by digital, video and educational material.

Key outputs included:

- Rosetta Strato digital campaign
- Campaign visual identity and design
- Campaign video
- Charity campaign presence
- Educational and public-engagement content
- Association with UNAWE educational outreach

## Impact

The project's impact was primarily through **communication and engagement**.

Rather than attempting to reproduce the scientific work of the Rosetta mission,
the campaign focused on communicating its significance and making the story
accessible to wider audiences.

It demonstrates how creative communication can extend the reach of space
science beyond specialist audiences.

## Lessons learned

The Rosetta Strato campaign illustrates several principles relevant to space
and science communication:

### 1. Start with the story

Major scientific projects often contain compelling narratives that can provide
the structure for public communication.

### 2. Use design to reduce barriers

Good visual communication can make technically complex subjects easier to
approach without requiring audiences to understand the underlying science in
advance.

### 3. Connect communication to action

A campaign can move beyond awareness by giving audiences a meaningful way to
participate, such as educational engagement or charitable support.

### 4. Treat space as a human story

Space exploration is ultimately carried out by people, organisations and
communities. Communicating those stories can make technically sophisticated
missions much more relatable.

## Significance

Rosetta Strato is an example of how **space exploration, digital design and
science communication can be brought together within a single campaign**.

The project used one of the most engaging stories in modern planetary
exploration — Rosetta's journey to a comet and the deployment of Philae — as a
foundation for public-facing communication.

Its lasting value lies not only in the campaign itself, but in demonstrating
the potential of creative communication to make ambitious scientific and
engineering projects accessible to broader audiences.

SEPPCoN: Survey of the Ensemble Physical Properties of Cometary Nuclei

Collaborative observational programme investigating the physical and surface properties of Jupiter-family comet nuclei through thermal-infrared observations from the Spitzer Space Telescope and complementary ground-based visible-light measurements.

Examples of processed optical R-band imaging of three comets successfully detected at the ESO 3.6-m NTT telescope in May 2007. Comet Lovas 1 shows clear signs of activity, whereas comets NEAT and Klemola appear unresolved.

Contributed to a collaborative survey of roughly 100 Jupiter-family comets, combining thermal-infrared and visible-light observations to constrain nucleus sizes, albedos and thermal properties across a substantial fraction of the known population.

## Overview

SEPPCoN, the **Survey of the Ensemble Physical Properties of Cometary Nuclei**,
was a collaborative programme investigating the physical characteristics of
Jupiter-family comet nuclei.

Jupiter-family comets are short-period comets whose orbits are strongly shaped
by Jupiter. Their nuclei are relatively primitive Solar System bodies, making
them useful targets for studying the composition, structure and evolutionary
history of material left from planet formation.

The programme combined thermal-infrared measurements from the **Spitzer Space
Telescope** with visible-light observations from ground-based telescopes. This
multi-wavelength approach was used to constrain nucleus sizes, surface
reflectivity and thermal behaviour for a large sample of cometary nuclei.

## Research objectives

The project aimed to improve population-level understanding of Jupiter-family
comets by addressing several connected questions:

- What are the typical sizes and geometric albedos of cometary nuclei?
- Is there evidence that albedo varies systematically with nucleus size?
- What do thermal measurements reveal about the surface properties of nuclei?
- How does the size distribution of observed nuclei inform models of cometary
  evolution and the small-body populations of the Solar System?
- Can thermal and visible-light observations be combined to reduce uncertainty
  in estimates of nucleus size and reflectivity?

## Observations

### Spitzer Space Telescope

Spitzer observations measured thermal emission from cometary nuclei at
mid-infrared wavelengths. The programme used imaging capabilities associated
with the Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) and the Multiband Imaging Photometer for
Spitzer (MIPS), including observations around 16 and 22 micrometres.

Thermal-infrared observations are particularly valuable because they provide a
constraint on the heat emitted by a body. When combined with visible-light
measurements, they help break the degeneracy between an object's physical size
and its surface reflectivity.

A small, bright object and a larger, dark object can have similar brightness in
visible light. Thermal emission provides additional information that enables
more reliable estimates of effective radius and geometric albedo.

### Ground-based optical observations

Ground-based visible-light observations complemented the Spitzer measurements.
They provided photometry and contextual observations needed to interpret the
thermal signal and separate nucleus properties from the effects of cometary
activity, dust and observing geometry.

Together, the space- and ground-based observations supported a more robust
physical characterisation of individual comets and the wider Jupiter-family
comet population.

## Methods

The analysis combined thermal-infrared fluxes with optical photometry to derive
physical parameters for cometary nuclei.

Key steps included:

- Measuring thermal emission at mid-infrared wavelengths.
- Using visible-light observations to constrain reflected sunlight.
- Applying thermal models to estimate effective nucleus radii.
- Calculating geometric albedos from combined thermal and optical constraints.
- Comparing derived properties across the survey sample.
- Examining the cumulative size distribution of Jupiter-family comet nuclei.

The programme also considered thermal inertia, a property describing how quickly
a material responds to heating and cooling. Low thermal inertia is consistent
with a porous, dusty and weakly conducting surface layer.

## Findings

SEPPCoN results indicated that many Jupiter-family comet nuclei have low thermal
inertia, consistent with surfaces that are porous, dusty and relatively poor
conductors of heat.

Preliminary analysis of the cumulative size distribution found a power-law slope
similar to results from visible-light studies. This suggested that there was no
strong evidence for a systematic relationship between nucleus size and albedo
across the observed sample.

The survey provided a larger and more consistently analysed dataset for
evaluating the physical properties of Jupiter-family comet nuclei than was
available from isolated observations alone.

## My role

I contributed to the SEPPCoN collaboration while associated with the Centre for
Astrophysics and Planetary Science at the University of Kent.

My involvement formed part of doctoral research activity in planetary science
and astronomical observation. The programme brought together collaborators
working on Spitzer thermal-infrared data, ground-based optical measurements,
physical modelling and population-level analysis of Jupiter-family comets.

## Scientific context

Cometary nuclei preserve material from the early Solar System and may retain
information about the environments in which planetesimals formed. Understanding
their size distribution, albedo and thermal properties helps connect present-day
comet observations with models of Solar System evolution.

Jupiter-family comets are especially important because their orbits bring them
into the inner Solar System, where their nuclei can be studied in detail.
However, activity, dust and observational selection effects can complicate
physical interpretation. Combining thermal-infrared and visible-light
measurements provides a stronger basis for estimating intrinsic nucleus
properties.

## Limitations

Cometary nuclei are difficult targets because activity can obscure or alter the
signal from the solid nucleus. Thermal models also depend on assumptions about
surface roughness, emissivity, rotation, observing geometry and thermal
properties.

The project therefore provides population-level constraints rather than a
complete physical description of every observed comet. Derived radii and
albedos should be interpreted alongside model assumptions and the quality of
the available optical and thermal measurements.

## Related outputs

### Results from the SEPPCoN Survey of Jupiter-Family Comets

## Overview

The **SGAC Find An Asteroid Search Campaign** was a volunteer asteroid-hunting activity run through the Space Generation Advisory Council (SGAC), the global network for students and young professionals in the space sector.

Scripted a short ESA documentary on Vega launch infrastructure
Translated engineering and materials-science concepts for a general audience

## Overview

**Getting Vega's Launch Tower Moving** is a short European Space Agency
documentary about the mobile launch tower used to prepare Vega rockets at
Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana.

The film explores the engineering required to move the large service structure
away from the launch vehicle before liftoff. Although the operation appears
straightforward from a distance, it depends on careful structural design,
materials engineering, mechanical systems and launch-site operations.

I contributed script development for the film through Design & Data, helping
translate specialised engineering work into a clear story for a general
audience.

## The subject

Vega is Europe’s launcher for small satellite payloads. At the launch pad, the
rocket is assembled and checked inside a mobile building that protects
personnel, equipment and the launch vehicle during preparation.

Before launch, the entire structure moves away from the rocket, leaving the
vehicle exposed and ready for liftoff. ESA describes the mobile building as
approximately 50 metres tall and weighing more than 1,000 tonnes.

The film focuses on the practical question behind this operation:

> How do you safely move a 1,000-tonne launch tower while maintaining the
> precision, reliability and safety required for a space launch campaign?

## Communications challenge

Launch infrastructure is essential to every mission but is often less visible
than the rocket itself.

The editorial challenge was to make a highly technical process understandable
without reducing it to spectacle. The script needed to connect:

- The familiar visual moment of a launch tower rolling away.
- The scale and mass of the mobile service structure.
- The materials and engineering decisions required for reliable movement.
- The safety requirements of launch operations.
- Vega’s role in Europe’s space transportation system.

The resulting narrative used the movement of the tower as an entry point into
the wider systems engineering that makes a launch possible.

## My role

## Overview

**Vortex** is a wind-resource and site-assessment service that uses
meteorological modelling and climate data to support renewable-energy project
development.

This project communicated how Vortex uses information from the **Copernicus
Climate Change Service** (C3S), implemented by the European Centre for
Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), to provide wind information for
planning and safeguarding wind-energy projects.

I contributed editorial and science-communication work through Design & Data,
helping turn a technical climate-services use case into a clear story about the
practical value of climate data for renewable-energy decisions.

## Context

Wind-energy projects depend on reliable estimates of wind conditions over long
periods. Developers need to understand expected energy yield, local terrain
effects, seasonal variation, extreme conditions and the uncertainty associated
with a proposed site.

Direct wind measurements are valuable, but they can be limited in geographic
coverage and historical duration. Climate reanalysis datasets provide a
consistent, long-term record that can be combined with local modelling to
support site selection, energy-yield estimates and project risk assessment.

Vortex provides online “Wind & Site” information derived from mesoscale
meteorological modelling and ERA5 climate reanalysis data produced by ECMWF.

## The challenge

The project needed to communicate a complex technical chain in practical terms:

Global climate reanalysis
→ high-resolution meteorological modelling
→ site-specific wind information
→ renewable-energy development decisions

This meant explaining why climate data matters to audiences beyond meteorology
and Earth observation, including wind-farm developers, investors, engineers,
planners and policy stakeholders.

The editorial challenge was to make the connection between climate data and
energy infrastructure concrete:

- How can a long-term climate record help estimate wind resources?
- Why do local terrain and atmospheric conditions matter?
- What does downscaling add beyond coarse global information?
- How can climate services reduce uncertainty during project development?
- How can data support more resilient renewable-energy investment?

## Vortex and C3S

Vortex uses C3S data for its online wind-modelling services.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service provides climate information based on
observations, models and reanalysis. ECMWF operates C3S on behalf of the
European Union and produces the ERA5 global climate reanalysis dataset used in
many climate-service applications.

Vortex combines large-scale climate information with mesoscale modelling to
produce wind-resource data at a more useful spatial scale for energy projects.
Its services are designed to support planning and risk management across the
renewable-energy project lifecycle.

## My role

I worked as an **Editor and science communicator** through Design & Data.

My contribution supported the editorial development of an ECMWF and Copernicus
Climate Change Service user story, explaining how Vortex applied climate data
to a commercial and operational renewable-energy context.

The work included:

- Translating climate-service concepts into accessible language.
- Developing a clear narrative around renewable-energy decision-making.
- Explaining the relationship between reanalysis, modelling and wind-resource
  assessment.
- Supporting video and multimedia communication.
- Connecting technical data infrastructure with its social, commercial and
  environmental value.

## Editorial approach

The central editorial idea was simple:

> Climate data helps turn uncertainty about future energy resources into better
> evidence for renewable-energy decisions.

Rather than presenting ERA5 or mesoscale modelling as isolated technical
products, the story followed the route from data to outcome.

```text
Climate record
→ Wind conditions
→ Site assessment
→ Energy-yield estimate
→ Project planning and investment
```

This approach gave the viewer a practical reason to care about climate
services: they help developers make more informed choices when designing
renewable-energy infrastructure.

## Wind-resource modelling

Wind conditions vary across time and geography. A site can be affected by
large-scale weather patterns, seasonal shifts, land cover, elevation, terrain,
surface roughness and local flow effects.

Vortex uses numerical weather modelling to translate broader atmospheric
conditions into higher-resolution wind information. Its modelling workflow
uses Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF)-based approaches and
high-performance computing to downscale atmospheric data for wind-resource
applications.

The resulting information can be used where direct measurements are limited,
while still requiring appropriate validation, local expertise and careful
interpretation in project-specific decisions.

## Outcomes

The completed case study and video supported public and professional
communication around the use of Copernicus Climate Change Service data in the
renewable-energy sector.

Key outcomes included:

- An accessible explanation of a C3S climate-service application.
- Clearer communication of how wind-resource modelling supports wind-farm
  planning.
- A practical example of climate data contributing to renewable-energy
  development.
- Video material associated with the European State of the Climate event in
  April 2018.
- A reusable narrative linking Earth observation, climate science, energy
  systems and investment decisions.

## Limitations

This project concerned editorial communication and climate-service storytelling.
It did not involve developing the Vortex platform, producing ERA5 itself or
operating the underlying wind models.

Modelled wind-resource information is not a substitute for all on-site
measurement and engineering assessment. Results depend on data quality, model
configuration, local terrain, observation availability and the specific
requirements of a proposed energy project.

## Overview

**Windy** was a communications project connected to the European Centre for
Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), the Copernicus programme and the use of
interactive visualisation to make environmental data easier to understand.

The work focused on explaining how complex forecast and monitoring data can be
made useful to non-specialist audiences through familiar, map-based interfaces.
Windy presents changing weather and environmental conditions as an interactive
global visualisation, allowing users to explore variables such as wind, rain,
cloud, temperature and air quality.

I contributed editorial and science-communication work through Design & Data,
supporting clear public storytelling around atmospheric data, Copernicus
services and the practical value of environmental information.

## Context

Weather and atmospheric information is technically complex. Forecasting systems
combine physics-based models with observations from satellites, weather
stations, aircraft, ships, balloons and other instruments.

For public audiences, the usefulness of this information depends not only on
scientific quality but on whether it can be understood and applied. Interactive
maps offer a practical way to show changing conditions across time and place.

Windy is a weather-visualisation service that displays a range of forecast
layers over an interactive global map. It uses ECMWF weather information
alongside other sources to present variables including wind, rain, lightning
and cloud types.

## The challenge

The communications challenge was to connect three different levels of the
story:

- **Scientific infrastructure:** ECMWF forecasting and Copernicus monitoring
  systems.
- **Environmental information:** weather, atmospheric composition, air quality
  and aerosol forecasts.
- **Public value:** a visual interface through which people can explore
  conditions relevant to daily life, travel, safety and environmental awareness.

This required translating terms such as atmospheric composition, particulate
matter, nitrogen dioxide, numerical modelling and forecast layers into clear,
practical language without overstating certainty or simplifying away the
underlying science.

## CAMS and ECMWF

The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (**CAMS**) provides information
about atmospheric composition, including air pollutants, aerosols and other
components that affect air quality, climate and human health.

ECMWF implements CAMS on behalf of the European Union as part of the Copernicus
Earth-observation programme.

CAMS combines atmospheric models with satellite and in-situ observations to
produce daily analyses and forecasts of atmospheric composition. Its data can
support work on air quality, dust transport, wildfire smoke, volcanic ash,
solar energy and climate-related environmental monitoring.

## Windy partnership

In 2019, CAMS partnered with Windy to bring global air-quality information to
the Windy web and smartphone platform.

The integration included forecasts for:

- Nitrogen dioxide.
- Fine particulate matter.
- Wind-blown dust.
- Sea salt aerosol.
- Volcanic ash.
- Biomass-burning pollution and smoke.

CAMS supplied daily forecasts, while Windy made the information accessible
through its visual map interface. Copernicus reported that Windy served around
800,000 users per day at the time the partnership was announced.

## My role

I worked as an **Editor and science communicator** through Design & Data.

My contribution supported editorial development and public-facing communication
around ECMWF, Copernicus and environmental-data visualisation. The work focused
on presenting atmospheric science in a way that retained technical credibility
while remaining useful to audiences outside specialist forecasting,
meteorological and Earth-observation communities.

This included helping shape narratives around:

- The relationship between weather forecasts and atmospheric monitoring.
- The role of ECMWF in producing and providing environmental information.
- The value of Copernicus services for public understanding and decision-making.
- How interactive visualisation can make large environmental datasets more
  approachable.
- The practical relevance of air-quality forecasts and atmospheric monitoring.

## Editorial approach

The communication approach was based on a simple principle:

> Environmental data becomes more useful when people can see where it applies,
> understand what it means and explore how it changes over time.

The project used map-based visualisation as the bridge between complex
forecasting infrastructure and everyday interpretation.

This approach helped frame atmospheric data not as an abstract technical
resource, but as information that can support decisions about health, travel,
outdoor activity, aviation, emergency response and environmental awareness.

## Outcomes

The work contributed to communications around the use of Copernicus and ECMWF
data in public-facing weather and environmental visualisation.

Key outcomes included:

- Clearer storytelling around atmospheric forecast data.
- Public-facing explanation of CAMS air-quality information.
- Support for communications linking ECMWF, Copernicus and Windy.
- Editorial framing of interactive environmental-data visualisation.
- Video and multimedia material associated with the project.

## Limitations

This project concerned editorial communication and public understanding of
environmental information. It did not involve producing ECMWF forecast models,
operating Copernicus services or developing the Windy platform itself.

Forecast and monitoring products remain subject to uncertainty, spatial
resolution limits, data availability and the interpretation constraints
associated with any environmental model. Public communication should therefore
help audiences understand both the value and the limits of forecast
information.

Queen Elizabeth Diamond Jubilee Wood (QEDJW) volunteering work

The Queen Elizabeth Diamond Jubilee Wood (QEDJW) lies in the National Forest in north-west Leicestershire, 24.1km (15 miles) from Leicester, 6.4km (4 miles) from Ashby-de-la-Zouch, 11.2km (7 miles) from Coalville, and close to the village of Normanton le Heath.
At the lake you'll find vegetation including bulrush and yellow iris.

Ongoing volunteering at one of the Woodland Trust's flagship Jubilee Woods, supporting the care of a young 116-hectare native woodland and wetland in the National Forest and helping keep it welcoming for people and wildlife.

## Overview

The Queen Elizabeth Diamond Jubilee Wood (QEDJW) is a large, young woodland
and wetland site in the National Forest, in north-west Leicestershire, close to
the village of Normanton le Heath. It was planted to mark the Queen's Diamond
Jubilee in 2012 and is the flagship site of the Woodland Trust's Jubilee Woods
project.

Since July 2024 I have volunteered here with the Woodland Trust, supporting
the practical work of caring for the wood and the experience of the people and
wildlife that use it.

## The wood at a glance

- **Location:** Normanton le Heath, in the National Forest, north-west
  Leicestershire (grid reference SK387122).
- **Distance:** about 24.1 km (15 miles) from Leicester, 6.4 km (4 miles) from
  Ashby-de-la-Zouch and 11.2 km (7 miles) from Coalville.
- **Size:** 116.38 hectares (287.57 acres).
- **Managed by:** the Woodland Trust.
- **Features:** on-site parking, public access, grassland, a lake, a bird
  hide, a pond-dipping platform and a large earth artwork.

## Landscape and habitats

QEDJW is more than a plantation. The site combines several habitats that
support one another:

- **New native woodland:** around 300,000 native broadleaf trees were planted
  between 2012 and 2015, including oak, field maple, silver birch, beech and
  hornbeam. The wood is now maturing into a beautiful young woodland.
- **Ancient woodland areas:** at the far end of the site, where bluebells and
  wood anemones carpet the ground in spring.
- **Wetland and lake:** home to vegetation such as bulrush and yellow iris,
  and an important draw for water birds.
- **Open grassland:** valuable for ground-nesting birds, butterflies and
  hares.

This mix of semi-natural ancient woodland, new planting and wetland makes the
site a good example of woodland creation working at landscape scale alongside
the wider National Forest.

## Wildlife

The wood is especially rewarding for birdwatchers:

- **Open ground:** skylarks and other ground-nesting birds.
- **The lake:** mute swans, little grebes, tufted ducks, terns and mallards.
- **Raptors:** buzzards and, rarely, the hen harrier.
- **At night:** tawny and barn owls hunting over the grassland.

In spring and summer the site is also good for butterflies, including the
striking marbled white. Deer and brown hares can be seen, and typical woodland
residents such as foxes, badgers, stoats and weasels share the site with
woodpeckers, bullfinches and tits.

## Art in the landscape

A striking feature of the wood is *Now & Then*, an earth artwork by artist
Rosie Leventon. It takes the form of a giant spiral descending into the ground,
and visitors can walk down the corkscrew. Oak and wild service trees have been
planted on the structure, so that over time it will become a shady, private
space within the wood. Along with the willow sculpture at the bird hide, the
artwork makes the site distinctive and popular with families.

## Visiting and access

- **Parking:** a signed car park on Heather Lane with space for 53 cars. It is
  locked overnight, opening at 8am and closing at 8pm from April to October and
  5pm from November to March.
- **Paths:** three waymarked, surfaced circular trails run from the car park to
  the lake. The main loop is suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs. A longer
  white route of about 3 km links the 61 Diamond Jubilee Groves, passes the
  lake and continues to the ancient woodland.
- **Gates:** pedestrian gates are an all-abilities design with a RADAR key
  padlock; others are standard kissing gates.
- **Terrain:** a number of long but gentle slopes on first entering the wood.
- **Access advice:** use the Heather Lane entrance rather than School Lane in
  Normanton le Heath, which is narrow.
- **Public transport:** there are no buses to Normanton le Heath itself, though
  services run from Leicester to Coalville and from Coalville to Ravenstone.
  The nearest railway stations are Burton, Tamworth and Loughborough, each
  around 24 to 26 km away.
- **Facilities:** there are no toilets on site; the nearest are in Coalville
  and Ashby.

*Opening hours, access arrangements and facilities can change, so check the
Woodland Trust website before visiting.*

## Things to do

- **Walking:** follow the trails to discover the artwork, groves, lake and
  ancient woodland.
- **Birdwatching:** the bird hide, funded by the Arts Council, sits just south
  of the lake and includes a willow sculpture.

Overview

The Queen Elizabeth Diamond Jubilee Wood (QEDJW) is a large, young woodland and wetland site in the National Forest, in north-west Leicestershire, close to the village of Normanton le Heath. It was planted to mark the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee in 2012 and is the flagship site of the Woodland Trust’s Jubilee Woods project.

Since July 2024 I have volunteered here with the Woodland Trust, supporting the practical work of caring for the wood and the experience of the people and wildlife that use it.

The wood at a glance

  • Location: Normanton le Heath, in the National Forest, north-west Leicestershire (grid reference SK387122).
  • Distance: about 24.1 km (15 miles) from Leicester, 6.4 km (4 miles) from Ashby-de-la-Zouch and 11.2 km (7 miles) from Coalville.
  • Size: 116.38 hectares (287.57 acres).
  • Managed by: the Woodland Trust.
  • Features: on-site parking, public access, grassland, a lake, a bird hide, a pond-dipping platform and a large earth artwork.

Landscape and habitats

QEDJW is more than a plantation. The site combines several habitats that support one another:

  • New native woodland: around 300,000 native broadleaf trees were planted between 2012 and 2015, including oak, field maple, silver birch, beech and hornbeam. The wood is now maturing into a beautiful young woodland.
  • Ancient woodland areas: at the far end of the site, where bluebells and wood anemones carpet the ground in spring.
  • Wetland and lake: home to vegetation such as bulrush and yellow iris, and an important draw for water birds.
  • Open grassland: valuable for ground-nesting birds, butterflies and hares.

This mix of semi-natural ancient woodland, new planting and wetland makes the site a good example of woodland creation working at landscape scale alongside the wider National Forest.

Wildlife

The wood is especially rewarding for birdwatchers:

  • Open ground: skylarks and other ground-nesting birds.
  • The lake: mute swans, little grebes, tufted ducks, terns and mallards.
  • Raptors: buzzards and, rarely, the hen harrier.
  • At night: tawny and barn owls hunting over the grassland.

In spring and summer the site is also good for butterflies, including the striking marbled white. Deer and brown hares can be seen, and typical woodland residents such as foxes, badgers, stoats and weasels share the site with woodpeckers, bullfinches and tits.

Art in the landscape

A striking feature of the wood is Now & Then, an earth artwork by artist Rosie Leventon. It takes the form of a giant spiral descending into the ground, and visitors can walk down the corkscrew. Oak and wild service trees have been planted on the structure, so that over time it will become a shady, private space within the wood. Along with the willow sculpture at the bird hide, the artwork makes the site distinctive and popular with families.

Visiting and access

  • Parking: a signed car park on Heather Lane with space for 53 cars. It is locked overnight, opening at 8am and closing at 8pm from April to October and 5pm from November to March.
  • Paths: three waymarked, surfaced circular trails run from the car park to the lake. The main loop is suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs. A longer white route of about 3 km links the 61 Diamond Jubilee Groves, passes the lake and continues to the ancient woodland.
  • Gates: pedestrian gates are an all-abilities design with a RADAR key padlock; others are standard kissing gates.
  • Terrain: a number of long but gentle slopes on first entering the wood.
  • Access advice: use the Heather Lane entrance rather than School Lane in Normanton le Heath, which is narrow.
  • Public transport: there are no buses to Normanton le Heath itself, though services run from Leicester to Coalville and from Coalville to Ravenstone. The nearest railway stations are Burton, Tamworth and Loughborough, each around 24 to 26 km away.
  • Facilities: there are no toilets on site; the nearest are in Coalville and Ashby.

Opening hours, access arrangements and facilities can change, so check the Woodland Trust website before visiting.

Things to do

  • Walking: follow the trails to discover the artwork, groves, lake and ancient woodland.
  • Birdwatching: the bird hide, funded by the Arts Council, sits just south of the lake and includes a willow sculpture.
  • Pond-dipping: a purpose-built platform on the western edge of the lake lets families catch and release minibeasts.
  • Dogs: welcome, following the Woodland Trust’s guidance for walking dogs in its woods.
  • Dedications: trees, benches or areas of woodland can be dedicated at the site.

They include flint shards and medieval pottery, and a Bronze Age palstave (axe) in mint condition found by a farm labourer in the 1970s. # Automotive

The automotive sector covers more than vehicles. It includes how they are designed, manufactured, powered, connected, used and eventually retired—and how they fit into wider mobility and energy systems.

My work in this sector focuses on making vehicle technology, electrification and low-emission mobility easier to understand. I translate technical and policy material into clear communication that supports informed decisions.

## Why it matters

Road transport affects emissions, air quality, energy demand, urban space and everyday mobility. The transition to lower-emission vehicles is therefore connected to climate goals, public health, energy systems and the design of towns and cities.

Electrification is an important part of this transition, but it is not the whole story. It also involves charging infrastructure, grid capacity, battery supply chains, vehicle efficiency, public transport, active travel and the way people use cars.

## My perspective

I approach automotive as part of a wider mobility and energy system.

A vehicle is not only a product. It is a node in a system involving energy generation, charging, roads, parking, freight, public transport and land use. Understanding those connections helps explain why decarbonising transport requires more than replacing one technology with another.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of automotive, energy, climate and communication. I am particularly interested in making technical subjects accessible without losing the engineering and policy context.

## The work I do

### Explaining vehicle technology

I help explain how vehicles work and how their technology is changing.

This can include electric powertrains, batteries, charging, efficiency, safety systems, connectivity and the materials and manufacturing processes behind them.

### Communicating low-emission mobility

The transition to low-emission transport involves technology, infrastructure, behaviour and policy. Clear communication needs to distinguish between what is available today, what is developing and what remains uncertain.

I help organisations explain their role in that transition, including the evidence behind their claims and the practical constraints involved.

### Making data meaningful

Vehicle and mobility data can reveal patterns in usage, efficiency, charging, emissions and network demand.

I help turn this data into accessible narratives and visual explanations, connecting it to questions about cost, reliability, environmental impact and user experience.

### Supporting informed decisions

Whether the audience is a driver, fleet operator, policymaker or manufacturer, transport decisions involve trade-offs. Clear communication can help people understand those trade-offs and make better-informed choices.
