# Built environment

The built environment is where climate, technology, design and everyday life meet. Buildings, streets, infrastructure and public spaces shape how people move, use energy, experience their surroundings and respond to environmental change.

My work in this sector focuses on making the built environment easier to understand and improve: communicating the role of buildings and infrastructure in sustainability, resilience and low-carbon transition, and helping make complex technical information accessible to the people who need it.

## Why it matters

The built environment has a major influence on emissions, resource use, health, accessibility and resilience. Buildings consume energy, embody carbon in their materials, shape transport patterns and affect how communities experience heat, flooding and air pollution.

A sustainable built environment is therefore not only about new construction. It also involves retrofitting existing buildings, improving infrastructure, planning places that reduce car dependency, and designing public spaces that support wellbeing and climate resilience.

## My perspective

I approach the built environment as a system of decisions: what is built, where, how it is operated, who it serves, and how it changes over time.

My interest is in making those decisions more visible and understandable. That includes explaining the relationship between buildings and energy, infrastructure and climate risk, urban design and wellbeing, and heritage and sustainable change.

I am particularly interested in how clear communication and digital tools can support better understanding of places, from local environmental impacts to the practical choices involved in retrofit, planning and resilience.

## The work I do

### Communicating places and systems

I help explain how buildings, infrastructure and urban systems work, and why their design and operation matter.

This can involve explaining energy use, retrofit approaches, planning decisions, transport connections, environmental risks or the relationship between a place and its wider context.

### Climate resilience and adaptation

The built environment needs to withstand changing conditions, including heat, flooding, drought and severe weather. Adaptation involves understanding risk, designing for resilience and making long-term decisions that do not lock in future problems.

I help communicate these issues in ways that make local relevance clear, without reducing complex risks to simplistic warnings.

### Low-carbon transition

Decarbonising the built environment involves operational energy, embodied carbon, retrofit, heating, transport and the materials used in construction.

I am interested in how organisations, public bodies and communities can communicate transition plans and progress honestly, including trade-offs, uncertainty and the difference between ambition and delivery.

### Digital tools and public understanding

Digital tools can make places and systems easier to explore. Catalogues, maps, visual narratives and accessible data-led resources can help people understand what exists, what is changing and what options are available.

My aim is to create useful entry points rather than duplicate detailed technical documentation.

# Climate

Climate change is both a scientific challenge and a practical one. It requires reducing greenhouse-gas emissions, preparing for impacts that are already underway, and communicating evidence in ways that support better decisions.

My work in this sector focuses on making climate information clearer, more relevant and more usable. I translate climate science, Earth-observation data and sustainability research into narratives, communication assets and digital tools that help people understand change and act on it.

## Why climate matters

Climate change affects weather, ecosystems, infrastructure, health, food systems and the places where people live. It is not only a long-term global problem: its effects are already visible through heat, drought, flooding, sea-level rise, changing seasons and pressure on natural systems.

Addressing it involves two connected tasks.

**Mitigation** means reducing or limiting greenhouse-gas emissions, or enhancing the removal and storage of carbon from the atmosphere. **Adaptation** means adjusting human and natural systems to actual or expected climate impacts, reducing vulnerability and building resilience. [258][259]

Neither replaces the other. Emissions reduction limits future change; adaptation helps societies live with the changes already locked in and those still to come.

## My perspective

I approach climate as a communication and translation challenge as much as a technical one.

Climate science can involve complex models, satellite observations, uncertainty ranges, emissions accounting and long time horizons. But its value depends on whether people can connect that evidence to the decisions they face: how a city plans for heat, how a business reduces risk, how a community prepares for flooding, or how policy responds to changing conditions.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of climate, sustainability, space and science communication. I am particularly interested in Earth observation and climate services: how satellite and environmental data can make climate impacts more tangible and support more informed action.

## The work I do

My climate work generally falls into four connected areas.

### Climate communication

I develop communication strategies, narratives and content that explain climate science, impacts and responses clearly.

This can include campaign planning, editorial content, video concepts, visual storytelling, event communication and materials for technical, policy and public audiences.

The aim is not simply to repeat the scale of the problem. It is to help audiences understand what is changing, why it matters, what evidence supports it, and what practical responses are available.

### Making climate data meaningful

Climate data becomes most useful when it is connected to a real question: How is temperature changing? What does that mean for heat risk? Where is flooding likely? How can a city, business or community prepare?

I help shape narratives and digital experiences that connect data to context. That includes explaining what a dataset represents, where its limitations lie, and why uncertainty should be communicated honestly rather than hidden.

### Earth observation and climate services

Satellite observations and environmental monitoring provide an important basis for understanding climate systems and supporting climate services.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service combines satellite and in-situ observations with climate models to provide information about past, present and future climate. It offers climate data, monitoring and tools intended to support adaptation and mitigation policy and practice. [253][257][264]

I am interested in how these data sources can be made more accessible, understandable and relevant to the people who need them.

### Sustainability and practical action

Climate work needs to connect evidence to action. That includes emissions reduction, resilience planning, low-carbon transition, environmental management and the practical decisions organisations and communities make.

I help turn technical or policy material into clear communication that supports understanding, engagement and delivery—without overstating certainty or promising simplistic solutions.

## Areas of focus

### Climate science and evidence

Clear climate communication starts with an accurate understanding of the evidence. That means distinguishing between observations, projections and scenarios, and being precise about confidence, uncertainty and limitations.

Climate information is most useful when it explains both the big picture and its local relevance. Global trends matter, but people also need to understand what changing conditions could mean for their own region, sector or community.

### Adaptation and resilience

Adaptation is about preparing for a changing climate: reducing exposure to hazards, strengthening resilience and making better long-term decisions.

This can involve flood risk, heat, drought, coastal change, infrastructure, health, agriculture and emergency planning. Effective adaptation depends not only on technical assessments, but also on clear communication that helps people understand risk and act on it.

### Mitigation and net zero

Mitigation concerns reducing emissions and transitioning towards lower-carbon systems. It spans energy, transport, buildings, industry, land use and consumption.

I am interested in how organisations and public bodies can communicate transition plans, progress and trade-offs honestly. Good mitigation communication avoids vague claims and explains what is actually changing, why, and over what timescale.

### Climate services and Earth observation

Climate services turn data into information that supports decisions. They can combine observations, models, forecasts and projections to help users understand risk and plan for the future.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service provides free and open access to climate data and tools through its Climate Data Store, alongside climate monitoring, seasonal forecasts and climate projections. [253][255][264]

I am particularly interested in how these services can be communicated to audiences beyond specialists, including policymakers, businesses, educators and the public.

## How I work

My approach combines scientific literacy, editorial judgement and practical delivery.

I begin by understanding the audience and the decision they need to make. Then I identify the core message, the evidence behind it and the most useful way to communicate it. Finally, I turn that into formats people can use: articles, videos, visual narratives, websites, event materials or digital tools.

I aim to be accurate about uncertainty, clear about sources and careful not to overstate what data can show. Good climate communication should make complexity easier to engage with—not make it disappear.

# Education

Education is about helping people understand the world and their place in it. It includes formal teaching, informal learning, public engagement, professional development and the digital tools that make knowledge easier to explore.

My work in this sector focuses on making complex subjects clearer and more engaging. I turn scientific, technical and environmental ideas into learning experiences, explanations and resources that support curiosity, understanding and confidence.

## Why it matters

Good education does more than transfer facts. It helps people develop the ability to ask questions, evaluate evidence, understand uncertainty and connect ideas to the world around them.

This matters particularly for science, climate and space. These subjects can feel distant or technical, yet they shape decisions about health, energy, the environment, technology and the future.

Education is also a bridge between research and public understanding. Clear explanations, well-designed resources and accessible digital experiences can help people move from curiosity to genuine understanding.

## My perspective

I approach education as translation with integrity.

The aim is not to simplify an idea until it becomes misleading. It is to identify the core concept, choose an appropriate starting point and build understanding step by step. That means being clear about what is known, what is uncertain and what questions remain open.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of science, sustainability, space and communication. I am particularly interested in helping people engage with subjects that can seem inaccessible: physics, Earth observation, climate systems and space science.

## The work I do

### Learning resources and explanations

I create explanations, guides and learning materials that make technical subjects accessible without losing accuracy.

This can include introductory explanations, visual narratives, teaching resources, interactive examples and materials designed for specific age groups or audiences.

### Science communication

Science communication and education often overlap. Both involve making evidence meaningful, but education places greater emphasis on progression: helping someone move from an initial question to a deeper understanding.

I develop content that supports that progression, whether the subject is space, climate, physics, environmental data or digital technology.

### Educational technology

Digital tools can support learning when they are designed around a clear educational purpose. They can help people explore data, test ideas, visualise systems and see the consequences of different assumptions.

I build or shape lightweight digital resources that make information easier to explore, while keeping the underlying science and limitations visible.

### Public engagement

Public engagement is education outside the classroom. Talks, exhibitions, community projects, online resources and events can all help people encounter new ideas in ways that feel relevant to their lives.

I am interested in work that connects research to everyday experience, particularly around climate, space and the environment.

I build or shape lightweight digital resources that make information easier to explore, while keeping the underlying science and limitations visible.

# Energy

Energy systems underpin modern life. They power homes, industry, transport and digital infrastructure, and they are central to the transition away from fossil fuels.

My work in this sector focuses on making energy systems and decarbonisation easier to understand. I translate technical, policy and data-led material into clear communication that explains what is changing, why it matters and what practical choices are involved.

## Why it matters

Decarbonising energy is one of the central tasks of climate mitigation. It involves changing how electricity is generated, how buildings are heated, how transport is powered and how industry uses energy.

This is not only a technology challenge. It also involves infrastructure, markets, regulation, planning, public acceptance and the practical realities of maintaining reliable services during transition.

A credible energy transition needs to explain both the opportunities and the constraints: renewable generation, grid flexibility, storage, electrification, efficiency and the continuing need for reliable, affordable energy.

## My perspective

I approach energy as a system, not a collection of isolated technologies.

Solar panels, wind turbines, batteries, heat pumps, grids and electric vehicles are connected. Their value depends on how they work together, how demand changes over time, and how the system remains reliable as it decarbonises.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of energy, climate, sustainability and communication. I am particularly interested in making technical systems understandable without oversimplifying the engineering, economics or policy context.

## The work I do

### Explaining energy systems

I help explain how energy is generated, moved, stored and used.

This can include renewable generation, electricity grids, storage, heat, transport electrification, industrial energy use and the interactions between them.

The aim is to make the system legible: showing not only individual technologies, but how they fit together and what they enable.

### Communicating decarbonisation

Decarbonisation involves difficult choices and long timescales. Clear communication needs to distinguish between ambition, policy, deployment and delivered outcomes.

I help organisations and projects explain their role in the transition, including what they are doing, why it matters, what evidence supports it and what limitations remain.

### Making data meaningful

Energy data can reveal patterns in generation, demand, emissions and system performance. But raw data alone rarely changes understanding.

I help turn data into accessible narratives and visual explanations, connecting numbers to real-world questions such as reliability, cost, emissions, resilience and local impact.

### Supporting public understanding

Energy transition affects people directly: through bills, planning decisions, local infrastructure, transport and the reliability of everyday services.

Clear communication can help people engage with those decisions more confidently, understanding both the need for change and the practical questions involved in delivering it.

# Environment

The environment is the living and physical world that supports human life: ecosystems, biodiversity, air, water, land and the processes that connect them.

My work in this sector focuses on making environmental change and environmental data easier to understand. I translate scientific research, Earth observation and sustainability issues into clear narratives, visual communication and digital resources.

## Why it matters

Healthy ecosystems support clean air, clean water, food production, flood regulation, carbon storage and wellbeing. Environmental degradation affects all of these systems, with consequences for both nature and people.

Environmental challenges are interconnected. Air pollution affects health and ecosystems; water management affects biodiversity and resilience; biodiversity loss weakens the systems that regulate climate and support livelihoods. Integrated action across climate, biodiversity and pollution is therefore essential. [279]

## My perspective

I approach the environment as a system of relationships rather than a set of separate issues.

Air, water, land, wildlife and human activity are connected. Understanding those connections helps explain why environmental protection is not only about protecting individual species or places, but about maintaining the systems that support life.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of environment, climate, space and science communication. I am particularly interested in Earth observation: how satellite and environmental data can make change visible, support monitoring and inform practical action.

## The work I do

### Environmental communication

I help explain environmental issues in ways that are accurate, engaging and relevant to their audience.

This can include explaining ecosystems, pollution, conservation, environmental policy, monitoring data or the relationship between local places and wider environmental systems.

### Making environmental data meaningful

Environmental data can reveal patterns that are difficult to see directly: changing air quality, land use, water conditions, habitat loss or the effects of extreme weather.

I help turn data into narratives and visual explanations that make those patterns understandable, while being clear about uncertainty and limitations.

### Earth observation for environmental understanding

Satellite observations provide a consistent view of environmental change across large areas and over time. They can support monitoring of land, oceans, atmosphere and emergency-response needs.

I am interested in how Earth-observation data can support environmental monitoring, public understanding and practical decision-making.

### Conservation and sustainability

Environmental work is not only about describing problems. It is also about identifying practical responses: protecting habitats, reducing pollution, restoring ecosystems and managing resources sustainably.

I help communicate these responses in ways that are grounded in evidence and realistic about trade-offs.

# Fisheries

Fisheries connect marine ecosystems, food systems, coastal communities and economic activity. They involve the management of wild fish stocks, the farming of aquatic organisms, seafood supply chains and the policies that shape how these systems are used.

My work in this sector focuses on making fisheries science, management and sustainability easier to understand. I translate technical and policy material into clear communication that respects both ecological complexity and the people whose livelihoods depend on it.

## Why it matters

Fisheries are part of wider marine ecosystems. Their long-term viability depends on healthy stocks, functioning habitats, effective management and an understanding of the pressures facing ocean systems.

Sustainable fisheries aim to maintain biological and economic productivity over the long term without causing ecological changes that reduce options for future generations. 

Aquaculture is the farming of aquatic organisms, including fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants. It is distinct from capture fisheries, although the two are connected through seafood systems, markets and marine resource management. 

## My perspective

I approach fisheries as a system involving ecology, evidence, livelihoods and governance.

Fish stocks are not isolated resources. They are part of ecosystems affected by fishing pressure, habitat condition, pollution, climate change and management decisions. Effective fisheries management brings together information, analysis, consultation, regulation and implementation to support the long-term sustainable use of fisheries resources. 

My interest is in making these relationships clear: showing how science informs management, how management affects ecosystems and communities, and why uncertainty needs to be handled honestly.

## The work I do

### Fisheries and marine communication

I help explain fisheries science, management and sustainability in ways that are accessible without being simplistic.

This can include explaining stock assessment, quotas, fishing pressure, aquaculture, seafood traceability or the relationship between fisheries and wider ocean health.

### Making data meaningful

Fisheries rely on data: catch records, survey data, stock assessments, environmental observations and management indicators.

I help turn this information into clear narratives and visual explanations, showing what the data can tell us, what it cannot, and why uncertainty matters.

### Communicating sustainability

Sustainability in fisheries involves ecological, economic and social considerations. It is not only about the quantity of fish caught; it also concerns ecosystem health, community livelihoods, food supply and long-term resilience.

I help communicate these connections without reducing complex issues to simple labels.

### Supporting informed decisions

Fisheries management affects fishers, coastal communities, regulators, scientists and consumers. Clear communication can help these audiences understand the evidence, trade-offs and practical implications of different approaches.

# Health

Health is shaped by more than healthcare. It is influenced by the places people live, the air they breathe, the water they drink, the information they receive and the systems that support them.

My work in this sector focuses on making health information clearer and more usable. I translate public-health, clinical and data-led material into communication that supports understanding, engagement and better decisions.

## Why it matters

Health is connected to environment, climate, education and technology. Air pollution, extreme heat, flooding, unequal access to services and misinformation all affect health outcomes.

Public health depends not only on treatment, but also on prevention, early awareness, reliable information and the ability of people and services to respond effectively. Clear communication is therefore part of the system, not an optional extra.

## My perspective

I approach health as a system involving people, evidence, services and context.

A health message is most useful when it is accurate, accessible and relevant to the person receiving it. That means explaining what is known, what is uncertain and what practical action is appropriate—without creating unnecessary fear or false reassurance.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of health, environment, climate and communication. I am particularly interested in how data, digital tools and clear narratives can support public understanding and more effective services.

## The work I do

### Health communication

I help explain health topics in ways that are accurate, accessible and appropriate for their audience.

This can include public-health messaging, service information, campaign content, data explanations and materials for clinical, community or policy audiences.

### Making health data meaningful

Health data can reveal patterns in disease, service use, risk, access and outcomes. But data alone does not create understanding.

I help turn data into clear narratives and visual explanations, connecting evidence to real-world questions while respecting privacy, uncertainty and context.

### Climate, environment and health

Environmental conditions affect health. Air quality, heat, flooding, water quality and climate-related hazards can influence both immediate health risks and longer-term wellbeing.

I am interested in communication that makes these connections clear, helping people and organisations understand risk and prepare effectively.

### Digital tools and information

Digital tools can support health communication when they make reliable information easier to find, understand and act on.

My focus is on clarity, accessibility and appropriate use of evidence. A useful health tool should help people make informed decisions, not replace professional advice or oversimplify complex issues.

# Logistics

Logistics is the system that moves goods, materials and information from where they are produced to where they are needed. It connects suppliers, manufacturers, warehouses, transport networks, retailers and customers.

My work in this sector focuses on making logistics systems and their sustainability challenges easier to understand. I translate operational, environmental and data-led material into clear communication and practical digital resources.

## Why it matters

Logistics affects almost every part of modern life. It determines how food reaches shops, how materials reach construction sites, how products reach customers and how emergency supplies reach communities.

It also has a significant environmental footprint. Freight, warehousing and distribution involve energy use, emissions, land use and infrastructure decisions. Improving logistics therefore matters for efficiency, resilience and climate goals.

## My perspective

I approach logistics as a system of flows: goods, vehicles, people, data and decisions.

A delivery is not just a journey from A to B. It is the result of demand, inventory, routing, storage, infrastructure, timing and coordination. Understanding those connections helps explain why small changes can have wide effects.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of logistics, sustainability, climate and communication. I am particularly interested in how data and digital tools can make complex operations more visible and support better decisions.

## The work I do

### Explaining supply chains

I help explain how supply chains work and where their risks and opportunities lie.

This can include sourcing, production, warehousing, distribution, last-mile delivery, inventory and the relationships between different parts of a network.

### Communicating sustainability

Logistics decarbonisation involves vehicle technology, route planning, consolidation, modal shift, warehouse energy use and operational efficiency.

I help organisations explain what they are doing, why it matters and what evidence supports their progress, without overstating claims or ignoring trade-offs.

### Making operational data meaningful

Logistics generates data about movements, deliveries, inventory, emissions, delays and capacity. The value comes from turning that data into insight.

I help create clear narratives and visual explanations that connect operational data to practical questions: reliability, cost, resilience, emissions and customer experience.

### Digital tools and visibility

Digital tools can make logistics systems easier to understand and manage. Catalogues, dashboards, maps and data-led resources can help people see what is happening across a network.

My focus is on clarity and usefulness: helping people understand the system rather than adding another layer of complexity.

# Marine

The marine environment covers oceans, seas, coasts and the systems that connect them. It includes marine science, ocean observation, conservation, maritime activity and the policies that shape how these systems are used and protected.

## Why it matters

Oceans regulate climate, support biodiversity, provide food and livelihoods, and influence weather and coastal resilience. They are also affected by warming, acidification, pollution, habitat loss and changing patterns of use.

## My perspective

I approach the marine environment as a dynamic system rather than a distant backdrop.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of marine science, climate, Earth observation and communication. I am particularly interested in how satellite and ocean data can make large-scale change more tangible and relevant.

### Ocean and coastal communication

I help explain marine science and ocean issues in ways that are accurate and engaging.

This can include ocean circulation, sea-level rise, coastal change, marine ecosystems, ocean observation and the relationship between oceans and climate.

### Making ocean data meaningful

Marine conservation involves protecting ecosystems while recognising the importance of oceans for food, transport, recreation and economic activity.

# Space

Space is where scientific curiosity meets practical value on Earth. Satellites observe weather, oceans, land, ice and the atmosphere; missions test new technologies; and space-derived data increasingly informs climate action, emergency response, policy and public understanding.

My work in this sector focuses on making that value visible and usable. I translate complex missions, Earth-observation data and technical research into clear stories, communication assets and digital tools—without losing the scientific accuracy or uncertainty behind them.

## Why space matters

Space is often imagined as distant and abstract, but much of its most immediate value comes from looking back at Earth.

Satellite observations provide a consistent, global view that is difficult to obtain from the ground. They can monitor weather systems, oceans, forests, ice, air quality and atmospheric composition across regions where ground-based measurements are sparse or unavailable.

For example, ESA’s Aeolus mission used a Doppler wind lidar to provide global profiles of wind from the surface up to around 30 km, supporting weather forecasting and research into atmospheric dynamics.

Europe’s Copernicus Sentinel missions similarly observe land, ocean, atmosphere and emergency-response needs. Sentinel-1 provides radar observations of land, sea ice, oceans and marine environments; Sentinel-3 measures sea and land surface temperature, ocean colour and sea-surface topography; and atmospheric missions monitor gases and aerosols relevant to air quality and climate.

The challenge is rarely whether the data exists. It is helping people understand what it means, what it can and cannot tell them, and how it should inform decisions.

## My perspective

I approach space as a communication and translation problem as much as a technology problem.

A mission may involve sophisticated instrumentation, orbital mechanics, materials science, data processing and international collaboration. But its public value depends on whether different audiences can understand why it matters: scientists, policymakers, journalists, students, partners and the wider public.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of space, sustainability and science communication. I am particularly interested in Earth observation: how satellite data can make environmental and climate processes more tangible, and how clear communication can turn technical capability into public understanding and practical action.

## The work I do

My space work generally falls into four connected areas.

### Mission and Earth-observation communication

I develop communication strategies, narratives and content that explain missions, instruments and data in ways that are accurate and engaging.

This can include campaign planning, video concepts, editorial content, visual storytelling, social-media assets and materials for technical and non-technical audiences.

The aim is not simply to describe what a mission does. It is to show why it exists, what problem it addresses, how its data is used, and what difference it can make.

### Making satellite data meaningful

Satellite data becomes most useful when it is connected to a question people care about: How is the climate changing? Where is flooding likely? What is happening to air quality? How can communities prepare for environmental risk?

I help shape narratives and digital experiences that connect observations to context. That includes explaining what a measurement represents, where its limitations lie, and why uncertainty is part of good science rather than a weakness.

### Science communication and public engagement

Space offers a powerful way into physics, geography, data literacy and environmental awareness. I create and support communication that makes complex subjects accessible without reducing them to slogans or oversimplified claims.

This includes explaining missions and instruments, framing the relevance of satellite observations, and helping audiences distinguish between what is known, what is uncertain and what remains an open question.

### Digital tools and knowledge sharing

Alongside communication work, I build digital tools and resources that make information easier to explore. These may include catalogues, data-led visualisations, educational resources or lightweight APIs that make structured information more reusable.

The goal is not to duplicate documentation. It is to provide useful entry points: helping people discover relevant work, understand its context and move on to the authoritative source.

## Areas of focus

### Earth observation

Earth observation is central to my interest in space. It connects orbital technology directly to environmental and societal questions.

Satellite systems can observe changes across land, ocean, ice and atmosphere. Copernicus Sentinel data, for example, supports applications ranging from land management and agriculture to marine monitoring, emergency response and climate services.

I am particularly interested in how these observations can support climate adaptation, environmental monitoring and place-based storytelling.

### Climate and sustainability

Space data is increasingly important for understanding and responding to climate change. Observations of the atmosphere, oceans, ice, land surface and extreme events can support monitoring, modelling, preparedness and communication.

The connection between space and climate is not only technical. Effective climate communication needs to make evidence meaningful at a human scale: showing what changing data means for particular places, communities and decisions.

### Mission communication

Space missions involve long development cycles, specialist teams and high levels of technical complexity. Communication has to make that work intelligible without turning it into marketing language.

I focus on clear narratives, credible explanations and assets that can be reused across channels. This includes helping audiences understand not only what a mission achieves, but also the research, testing and collaboration behind it.

### Space policy and the space economy

The space sector is also shaped by governance, international cooperation, regulation, sustainability and commercial development. These issues affect how space is used, who benefits from it, and how its risks are managed.

I am interested in making these discussions more accessible, particularly where they connect to Earth observation, climate services, responsible use of space and public value.

## How I work

My approach combines scientific literacy, editorial judgement and practical delivery.

I start by understanding the audience and the decision they need to make. Then I identify the core idea, the evidence behind it and the most useful way to communicate it. Finally, I turn that into formats people can actually use: articles, videos, visual narratives, websites, catalogues or digital tools.

I aim to be precise about uncertainty, careful with claims and clear about sources. Good space communication should make complexity easier to engage with—not make it disappear.

Space

Space is where scientific curiosity meets practical value on Earth. Satellites observe weather, oceans, land, ice and the atmosphere; missions test new technologies; and space-derived data increasingly informs climate action, emergency response, policy and public understanding.

My work in this sector focuses on making that value visible and usable. I translate complex missions, Earth-observation data and technical research into clear stories, communication assets and digital tools—without losing the scientific accuracy or uncertainty behind them.

Why space matters

Space is often imagined as distant and abstract, but much of its most immediate value comes from looking back at Earth.

Satellite observations provide a consistent, global view that is difficult to obtain from the ground. They can monitor weather systems, oceans, forests, ice, air quality and atmospheric composition across regions where ground-based measurements are sparse or unavailable.

For example, ESA’s Aeolus mission used a Doppler wind lidar to provide global profiles of wind from the surface up to around 30 km, supporting weather forecasting and research into atmospheric dynamics.

Europe’s Copernicus Sentinel missions similarly observe land, ocean, atmosphere and emergency-response needs. Sentinel-1 provides radar observations of land, sea ice, oceans and marine environments; Sentinel-3 measures sea and land surface temperature, ocean colour and sea-surface topography; and atmospheric missions monitor gases and aerosols relevant to air quality and climate.

The challenge is rarely whether the data exists. It is helping people understand what it means, what it can and cannot tell them, and how it should inform decisions.

My perspective

I approach space as a communication and translation problem as much as a technology problem.

A mission may involve sophisticated instrumentation, orbital mechanics, materials science, data processing and international collaboration. But its public value depends on whether different audiences can understand why it matters: scientists, policymakers, journalists, students, partners and the wider public.

My background is in physics, and my work sits at the intersection of space, sustainability and science communication. I am particularly interested in Earth observation: how satellite data can make environmental and climate processes more tangible, and how clear communication can turn technical capability into public understanding and practical action.

The work I do

My space work generally falls into four connected areas.

Mission and Earth-observation communication

I develop communication strategies, narratives and content that explain missions, instruments and data in ways that are accurate and engaging.

This can include campaign planning, video concepts, editorial content, visual storytelling, social-media assets and materials for technical and non-technical audiences.

The aim is not simply to describe what a mission does. It is to show why it exists, what problem it addresses, how its data is used, and what difference it can make.

Making satellite data meaningful

Satellite data becomes most useful when it is connected to a question people care about: How is the climate changing? Where is flooding likely? What is happening to air quality? How can communities prepare for environmental risk?

I help shape narratives and digital experiences that connect observations to context. That includes explaining what a measurement represents, where its limitations lie, and why uncertainty is part of good science rather than a weakness.

Science communication and public engagement

Space offers a powerful way into physics, geography, data literacy and environmental awareness. I create and support communication that makes complex subjects accessible without reducing them to slogans or oversimplified claims.

This includes explaining missions and instruments, framing the relevance of satellite observations, and helping audiences distinguish between what is known, what is uncertain and what remains an open question.

Digital tools and knowledge sharing

Alongside communication work, I build digital tools and resources that make information easier to explore. These may include catalogues, data-led visualisations, educational resources or lightweight APIs that make structured information more reusable.

The goal is not to duplicate documentation. It is to provide useful entry points: helping people discover relevant work, understand its context and move on to the authoritative source.

Areas of focus

Earth observation

Earth observation is central to my interest in space. It connects orbital technology directly to environmental and societal questions.

Satellite systems can observe changes across land, ocean, ice and atmosphere. Copernicus Sentinel data, for example, supports applications ranging from land management and agriculture to marine monitoring, emergency response and climate services.

I am particularly interested in how these observations can support climate adaptation, environmental monitoring and place-based storytelling.

Climate and sustainability

Space data is increasingly important for understanding and responding to climate change. Observations of the atmosphere, oceans, ice, land surface and extreme events can support monitoring, modelling, preparedness and communication.

The connection between space and climate is not only technical. Effective climate communication needs to make evidence meaningful at a human scale: showing what changing data means for particular places, communities and decisions.
